summary: At the Feast of Dedication, Jesus says His sheep are safe in His and the Father’s hands and declares, “I and My Father are one.” They take up stones.
key_insight: At the feast that remembered the temple being set apart for God again, Jesus called Himself the One “whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world” (10:36). The feast honored a consecrated building; Jesus claimed to be the One the Father had consecrated.
story: It was winter in Jerusalem, the time of the Feast of Dedication, and Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon’s porch. The Jews surrounded Him and said, “How long do You keep us in doubt? If You are the Christ, tell us plainly.”

Jesus answered, “I told you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in My Father’s name, they bear witness of Me.” They did not believe because they were not His sheep. “My sheep hear My voice, and I know them, and they follow Me. And I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish; neither shall anyone snatch them out of My hand.” The Father who gave them to Him is greater than all, and no one can snatch them out of the Father’s hand. “I and My Father are one.”

Again they picked up stones to stone Him. Jesus said, “Many good works I have shown you from My Father. For which of those works do you stone Me?” They answered that they were not stoning Him for a good work but for blasphemy, “because You, being a Man, make Yourself God.”

Jesus answered from their own Scriptures. Their law called those to whom the word of God came “gods,” and the Scripture cannot be broken. How then could they accuse of blasphemy the One “whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world,” because He said, “I am the Son of God”? If He was not doing His Father’s works, they need not believe Him. But if He was, they should believe the works, “that you may know and believe that the Father is in Me, and I in Him.”
Once more they tried to seize Him, but He escaped out of their hand.

scene.label: The Feast of Dedication
scene.text: This is Hanukkah. In 167 BC the Syrian king Antiochus IV Epiphanes defiled the temple and forced pagan worship on Jerusalem. Judas Maccabeus and his followers retook the city, and on the twenty-fifth of Kislev (December), 164 BC, they cleansed the temple and dedicated it again with eight days of celebration (1 Maccabees 4:52–59). The Jews kept the feast every year after that.

scene.label: A feast of lights
scene.text: Josephus, writing in the first century, calls the feast Lights, and lamps came to mark it. The well-known story of one jar of oil lasting eight days appears only in rabbinic writings from centuries later.

scene.label: Hopes of deliverance
scene.text: The feast remembered Jewish fighters who threw off a foreign king and freed the temple. With Rome now ruling, the demand “If You are the Christ, tell us plainly” likely carried political hopes as well as religious ones.

scene.label: Solomon’s porch
scene.text: A long covered colonnade on the east side of the temple courts, named for Solomon. John’s note that “it was winter” may explain why Jesus walked there, under cover. The first believers later gathered in the same place (Acts 3:11; 5:12).

scene.label: “You are gods”
scene.text: Jesus quotes Psalm 82:6, where God calls “gods” those who judged in His name (most take them to be Israel’s judges) and then condemns them for injustice. If Scripture could use that word for mere men, the charge of blasphemy against the One the Father sent does not follow. Jesus does not lower His claim; He ends by saying the Father is in Him and He in the Father.

witnesses.john: Only John records this visit. He sets many of Jesus’ Jerusalem scenes at the Jewish feasts, and here the feast of the temple’s rededication becomes the setting for Jesus’ claim to be the One the Father set apart and sent. John ties the scene back to the Good Shepherd (10:26–28), so the safety of the sheep and the oneness of the Son with the Father stand together.

seeing.reveals: Jesus claims a unity with the Father so close that His hand and the Father’s hand hold the same sheep. He is the Son whom the Father set apart and sent, and His works prove it.
seeing.living: Jesus’ promise belongs to those who hear His voice and follow Him: they shall never perish, and no one can snatch them away. Rest your security on His grip, not on your own, and keep listening for His voice.
seeing.ponder: When you fear losing your hold on God, what does it mean to you that He has not lost His hold on you?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus’ sheep are held by two hands, His and His Father’s, and no one can snatch them.
preaching.watch_for: The two hands in verses 28–29 are the hinge. The Son and the Father do the same work of keeping, which leads straight to “I and My Father are one” (v. 30). The crowd understood the claim; that is why they took up stones (v. 33).
